title: Yemen
hookLine: an ancient community with its own prayers, melodies and Torah readings

cards: A Shabbat morning in a Yemenite synagogue. The Torah scroll is open. A reader chants a verse in Hebrew, in a melody of its own, rising and falling.

Then he stops, and a young boy beside him chants the same verse again, this time in Aramaic. Verse by verse, Hebrew, then Aramaic, all the way through the reading. Nobody is rushing, not the reader and not the boy.

teach.b: Yemen sits at the bottom corner of the Arabian peninsula. Jews lived there for a very long time, and tradition tells of their arrival in the days of the Bible.
Far from the big centers of Jewish learning, they kept their own ways. First, the reading. That Aramaic voice is the Targum, an ancient translation of the Torah.
In many places it stopped being read aloud in the synagogue. Yemenite Jews kept the custom, and a child often reads the Targum, so the young learn by doing. Second, the prayers.
Yemenite Jews have their own prayer book, the Tiklal, with its own order and melodies, passed down mostly by ear, in families, in the same small synagogues. Third, the poetry.
A beloved Yemenite poet, Shalom Shabazi, wrote songs still sung at weddings and Shabbat tables, mixing Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic.

When the State of Israel was new, Jews from Yemen were flown there in an airlift people named after a verse from Exodus, where God tells Israel: "I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself."
People who had never seen an airplane, tradition says, recognized it from that verse. The melodies came along, and singers from Yemenite families carried them into new music.
And in Yemenite synagogues in Israel, a child may still stand beside the reader, ready with the Aramaic.

how: In Yemenite synagogues the Torah is read verse by verse with the Aramaic Targum, often chanted by a child, and prayers follow the Tiklal prayer book with melodies handed down in families.

games.q: you're in a Yemenite synagogue. the reader has just chanted a verse of the Torah in Hebrew. what comes next?
o: the same verse in Aramaic, often from a child.
games.why: Yemenite Jews kept the old custom of reading the Targum aloud, verse by verse, a custom that faded in many other places.

practice: Bring back the synagogue: the Hebrew verse, then the boy's voice with the same verse in Aramaic. Let your breath follow that pattern, one breath to hear, one to repeat.
Then think of one thing you learned by repeating after someone older, and hold them in mind.
